newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Make-or-break months for Sabena as rumours fly.
newsitem.headline: Make-or-break months for Sabena as rumours fly.

text.p: Belgian airline Sabena said on Wednesday the next half year would be decisive for its future but denied rumours that dominant shareholder Swissair was about to pull the plug and bankruptcy was imminent.
Rumours on Sabena's future started flying after Sabena chief executive Paul Reutlinger recently told his staff that Sabena had only six months to win back its shareholders' confidence.

"We have to show Swissair, the world of aviation, travel agencies that Sabena is on the upward trail again. We have six months to prove that the trend has been reversed and that we are aiming for profit again," spokesman Eric Platteau told Reuters.

On Tuesday Reutlinger told an informal meeting of leading aviation officials in Brussels that Swissair may write off its six billion Belgian francs ($179 million) investment, for a 49.5 percent stake in Sabena, this coming spring, but that this was no prelude to a total pull-out by the Swiss carrier.

But observers note Sabena not only recorded a two billion Belgian franc first-half loss but that its performance has remained below par due to a series of crippling strikes early last year which undermined passengers' confidence.
The lead article in the Sabena Actueel internal newsletter earlier this month, headlined "now or never", said that social peace was the "condition sine qua non for success".

Leading Belgian financial daily L'Echo on Wednesday reported rumours that Sabena would file for bankruptcy in six months, Swissair's partners would split up Sabena's intercontinental network and Richard Branson's Virgin Express would take over its European network.
"We categorically deny these totally unfounded rumours, they are unrealistic," Sabena spokesman Eric Platteau said.
He noted that according to Belgian law an extraordinary board meeting would have to be called to decide whether to continue activities, once half the company's equity had been used up.
"But there is absolutely no problem concerning finances or liquidity at Sabena," Platteau said.

He added that Swissair had in the last two months installed its commercial office at Sabena, signed far-reaching deals with Sabena on cargo, catering and frequent flyer programmes and had bought new planes with its Belgian partner.
"There are so many joint projects which they would not have done if they wanted to pull out six months later," Platteau said.
He added that without any hiccups, Sabena would still see a loss in 1997 but "certainly" return to profitability in 1998.
Swissair, which has an option to raise its stake in Sabena to about 60 percent after 2000, is seeking a return on capital employed of four percent in 1998 and eight percent in 2000.
Last October Reutlinger pushed through a savings plan which included job cuts, adjustments in flexibility and working conditions and a two-year wage freeze.

He is also trying to push through a plan to relocate pilots to a foreign country, possibly Switzerland, to avoid having to pay heavy Belgian social security charges and save up to two billion francs ($60 million) per year.
